statements.claim: Years later, when people asked what Krishna and Arjuna spoke of after the war, the answer began with a confession: everything Krishna had told him on the battlefield, Arjuna had forgotten.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli): Janamejaya asks what conversation took place between Kesava and Arjuna in the assembly rooms; Arjuna: 'What thy holy self said unto me at that time, O Kesava, through affection, has all been forgotten by me, O chief of men, in consequence of the fickleness of my mind.'

statements.claim: Arjuna, having recovered his kingdom, spent his days in joy in Krishna's company in the palace at Hastinapura, in rooms that seemed a piece of heaven, surrounded by relatives and attendants.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli): 'The son of Pritha (Arjuna), having recovered his own kingdom, joyously spent his time... in the company of Krishna... in that palace of celestial beauty' in rooms that 'looked... like a veritable portion of Heaven... surrounded by their relatives and attendants.'

statements.claim: Arjuna said Krishna's greatness and his form as the Lord of the universe had become known to him on the approach of battle, and that Krishna would soon be leaving for Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'thy greatness became known to me upon the approach of the battle... thy form also, as the Lord of the universe, then became known to me... Thou again, O Madhava, wilt repair to Dwaraka soon.'

statements.claim: Krishna embraced Arjuna and answered that it was exceedingly disagreeable to him to learn that Arjuna had not, from folly, received what was imparted; the recollection of all he had told him would not come to him now; the teaching was more than sufficient for understanding Brahma; he could not discourse on it again in detail, for he had spoken of Supreme Brahma while concentrated in yoga.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli), Krishna's reply: 'embraced Phalguna and replied... It is exceedingly disagreeable to me to learn that thou didst not, from folly, receive what I imparted. The recollection of all that I told thee on that occasion will not come to me now... That religion... is more than sufficient for understanding Brahma. I cannot discourse on it again in detail. I discoursed to thee on Supreme Brahma, having concentrated myself in Yoga.'

statements.claim: Krishna promised to recite an old history upon the same topic, by which Arjuna, listening with an understanding adapted to the teaching, might attain the highest end.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'I shalt now, however, recite to thee an old history upon the same topic... so that, with an understanding adapted to my teaching, thou mayst succeed in attaining to the highest end.'

statements.claim: In the old history, a Brahmana of irresistible energy had come to Krishna and Arjuna from the regions of Heaven, from the presence of the Grandsire, and was reverenced duly; asked about the religion of Emancipation — out of compassion for all creatures and not for his own good — he agreed to speak, asking that they listen with concentrated attention.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'a Brahmana came to us from the regions of Heaven. Of irresistible energy, he came from the regions of the Grandsire. He was duly reverenced by us... That which thou askest me, O Krishna, connected with the religion of Moksha (Emancipation), led by thy compassion for all creatures (and not for thy own good)... I shall now tell thee duly... Do thou listen with concentrated attention.'

statements.claim: The old history concerned a Brahmana named Kasyapa, foremost of all persons conversant with duties, who had heard of another Brahmana who had mastered the scriptures on the departure and reappearance of beings, possessed the direct knowledge yoga gives, knew the truths of the world, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, beheld the ends attained by embodied creatures, lived like one emancipated, had his senses under control, seemed to blaze with the resplendence of Brahma, could go everywhere at will, knew the science of disappearing at will, roved with invisible Siddhas and celestial musicians, and was unattached as the wind.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli), the Brahmana's narration: 'A Brahmana of the name of Kasyapa, possessed of penances and the foremost of all persons conversant with duties, came to a certain other Brahmana who had become conversant with all the mysteries of religion...' — followed by the full catalogue of the sage's attainments as rendered in the story.

statements.claim: Kasyapa, having heard of him, desired to see him; approaching the sage and seeing those wonderful attributes, he fell with a rapt heart at his feet and began to wait upon him with dutiful reverence.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'Kasyapa having heard of him truly, desired to see him... Kasyapa, moved by the desire of acquiring merit, fell, with a rapt heart, at the feet of the sage when he had seen all those wonderful attributes. Filled with wonder... Kasyapa began to wait upon that foremost of all Brahmanas, with the dutiful reverence.'

statements.claim: The old history Krishna promised would unroll through the days that followed into the teaching known as the Anugita; it is the tale of Kasyapa as told by the Brahmana of Heaven.
statements.evidence: Index/chain confirm Krishna 'instead narrates an old history (the Anugita)' and the MBh 14.16 passage places the Brahmana of Heaven's narration in answer to Krishna's enquiries (the inner tale is of Kasyapa approaching the sage). The closing sentence slightly compresses the nesting (the Brahmana of Heaven narrates to Krishna; within that narration the sage teaches Kasyapa), but 'told to Kasyapa' is a defensible shorthand for where the narration is headed and is connective framing, not a correction-worthy factual error.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims; prose tracks MBh 14.16 (Ganguli) nearly clause-for-clause. One minor nesting compression in the closing frame (see last statement).

statements.claim: By the time the Yadava clan had all but destroyed itself, there was almost no one left at Krishna's side; he had watched the course of his own maya run out to its end.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4 index: 'Uddhava recalls how, as the Yadavas destroyed themselves, Krishna sat at the foot of an ashvattha tree...'; SB 3.4.2: 'bhagavān svātma-māyāyā gatiṃ tām avalokya saḥ' — the Lord, seeing that course of his own maya.

statements.claim: Krishna walked to the bank of the Sarasvati, sipped the water, and sat down at the foot of an ashvattha tree.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (SB 3.4.2-10 rendered): 'The Lord... sipped the Sarasvati and sat at the foot of a tree'; index location: 'the bank of the Sarasvati, at the foot of an ashvattha tree.'

statements.claim: There Krishna told Uddhava to go to Badari, the hermitage in the north; Uddhava, unable to leave his feet, lingered and followed at a distance; Krishna found him there and said: I know your heart's desire; I grant you what is hard for others to attain.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (SB 3.4.2-10): 'he said to me, go to Badari. Yet, unable to leave his feet, I followed; and he, finding me there, told me: I know your heart's desire; I grant you what is hard for others to attain.' (Badari as the northern hermitage is standard identification consistent with the pack.)

statements.claim: Uddhava saw his Lord seated alone, contemplating — dark and radiant, free of all passion, eyes peaceful and touched with red, right foot resting on his left thigh.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.5-7: 'adrākṣam ekam āsīnaṃ vicinvan dayitaṃ patim' (I saw my beloved Lord seated alone, contemplating); 'śyāmāvadātaṃ virajaṃ praśāntāruṇa-locanam' (dark-and-radiant, passionless, tranquil reddish eyes); 'vāma ūrāv adhiśritya dakṣiṇāṅghri-saroruham' (right lotus foot resting on the left thigh).

statements.claim: Uddhava is the great devotee, the friend of Vyasa (Dvaipayana) himself, and bowed with joy, his head bent low.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.8-9: 'tasmin mahā-bhāgavato dvaipāyana-suhṛt-sakhā... pramoda-bhāvānata-kandharasya' — the great devotee, friend of Dvaipayana, neck bent with joyful emotion.

statements.claim: Krishna told Uddhava: This is the last of your births; my grace has come to you; what I spoke long ago to Brahma, seated on the lotus born from my navel at the beginning of creation, is what I give you now.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.11-12: 'sa eṣa sādho caramo bhavānām āsāditas te mad-anugraho yat' (this is the last of your births — my grace has been obtained by you); 'purā mayā proktam ajāya nābhye padme niṣaṇṇāya mamādi-sarge' (spoken by me long ago to the unborn Brahma seated on the lotus of my navel at the beginning of creation).

statements.claim: Uddhava praised Krishna — the one who acts without desire, whose birth and non-birth are beyond telling, the refuge of the distressed whom the frightened reach by fleeing from every fear, the one invoked in mantras, whose knowledge of the self is unbroken, complete and eternal.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.15-16: 'karmāṇy anīhasya bhavo 'bhavasya te durgāśrayo 'thāri-bhayāt palāyanam / mantreṣu māṃ vā upahūya yat tvam akuṇṭhitākhaṇḍa-sadātma-bodhaḥ' — desireless acts, birth and non-birth inconceivable, refuge of the distressed, invoked in mantras, unbroken complete eternal self-knowledge.

statements.claim: Krishna taught Uddhava the supreme knowledge that illuminates the secret of the self, and granted him the state hard for others to attain; the account in SB 3 is Uddhava's own recollection.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.17-18: 'jñānaṃ paraṃ svātma-rahaḥ-prakāśaṃ provāca kasmai bhagavān samagram' (the supreme knowledge revealing the secret of the self, taught completely); pack index: 'granted him the ancient teaching and the supreme state'; the passage is Uddhava speaking (śrī-uddhava uvāca), matching the story's 'Uddhava has left us his own account of that hour.'

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Dense Sanskrit pack (SB 3.4.2-18) maps cleanly onto the story's details; final 'whisper by a river' line is poetic atmosphere.

statements.claim: In the palace at Mathura, when Krishna wanted comfort carried to the people of his boyhood, he looked to Uddhava, his beloved devotee, his friend whose heart was fixed on him alone.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.1: 'tam āha bhagavān preṣṭhaṃ bhaktam ekāntinaṃ kvacit' — the Lord spoke to his dearest devotee, wholly fixed on him alone; index sets the episode in Mathura.

statements.claim: Krishna sent Uddhava with a message: 'Go to Vraja... Bring joy to my parents' — Nanda and Yashoda who had raised him; the summons of Kamsa's court had carried him away to Mathura.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.2: 'gacchoddhava vrajaṃ saumya pitror nau prītim āvaha' — go to Vraja, bring joy to our parents. (Nanda/Yashoda as his Vraja parents and Kamsa's summons as the cause of his removal to Mathura are canonical SB background consistent with the pack; not stated in the six excerpted verses but uncontested context.)

statements.claim: The women of Gokula had their minds fixed on Krishna; their very lives were given up for his sake; for his sake they had abandoned comfort, standing, even their own bodies; to them he was the dearest of all dear ones, and he was far away; they were keeping themselves alive only with great difficulty.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.3-5: 'tā man-manaskā tṛṣṭ-prāṇā mad-arthe tyakta-daihikāḥ / mayi tāḥ preyasāṃ preṣṭhe dūra-sthe gokula-striyaḥ / dhārayanty ati-kṛcchreṇa prāyaḥ prāṇān kathañcana' — minds fixed on me, lives given up, bodies abandoned for my sake; the Gokula women to whom I am dearest of the dear, far away, barely sustaining their lives with great difficulty.

statements.claim: Uddhava, who held no office, had been at Krishna's side through the long years in Mathura and had seen how Krishna grew quiet whenever the talk turned to Vrindavan — a single mention of the village could stop him mid-sentence.
statements.evidence: Not in the pack's six excerpted verses; invented-but-plausible connective backstory dramatizing the affection that 10.46.1-5 implies (Krishna's tender message to Vrindavan). No pack source contradicts it.

statements.claim: Uddhava accepted the charge, promising to tell Nanda and Yashoda of their son, carry Krishna's love to the women of Gokula, and not rest until he had consoled them; he made ready and set out for Vrindavan.
statements.evidence: The mission's substance is supported (SB 10.46.1-6 + chain to DKS_0503 where Uddhava arrives in Vrindavan); Uddhava's spoken acceptance and the travel details are connective narration not present in the excerpted verses.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. The gopis' message is rendered near-verbatim from SB 10.46.3-5; the opening paragraphs (Uddhava's rank, Krishna's demeanor) are acceptable connective backstory.

statements.claim: Uddhava reached Nanda's Vraja as the sun went down.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.7: 'prāpto nanda-vrajaṃ śrīmān nimlocati vibhāvasau' — he reached Nanda's Vraja as the sun was setting.

statements.claim: The village at dusk was alive: bulls scenting the cows bellowed and fought in the lanes, white calves leaped about so the settlement seemed dressed in them, and the women sang the auspicious deeds of Bala and Krishna.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.8-10: bulls fighting for the scent of cows ('vāsitārthe 'bhiyudhyadbhir... vṛṣaiḥ'), white calves leaping everywhere ('vilaṅghadbhir go-vatsair maṇḍitaṃ sitaiḥ'), women singing the auspicious deeds of Bala and Krishna ('gāyantībhiś ca karmāṇi śubhāni bala-kṛṣṇayoḥ').

statements.claim: Every home bore marks of worship of the fire, the sun, the guest, the cow, the Brahmana, the ancestors and the gods, and the forests around stood in full flower, loud with the calling of birds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.11-12: 'agny-arkātithi-go-vipra-pitṛ-devārcanānvitaiḥ' and 'sarvataḥ puṣpita-vanaṃ dvijāli-kula-nāditam.'

statements.claim: Nanda hurried to meet Uddhava, Krishna's own companion and beloved attendant, embraced him and honored him as he would have honored Vasudeva himself, pressed the finest food upon him and seated him comfortably on a couch; only then did he begin his questions.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.13-14: Nanda approached Uddhava, 'kṛṣṇasyānucaraṃ priyam', fed him 'paramānnena' and seated him 'kaśipau sukham'; pack excerpt: 'was embraced by Nanda and honored as Vasudeva himself'; Nanda's questions follow at vv. 15+.

statements.claim: Nanda asked whether his friend, the son of Shura, was well; said that by good fortune the sinner Kamsa had been killed with all his followers by the very evil he had done; asked whether Krishna remembered his mother, friends and playmates, and whether Govinda would ever come back to look upon his own people.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.15-18: 'kaccid aṅga mahā-bhāga sakhā naḥ śūra-nandanaḥ' (15); 'diṣṭyā kaṃso hataḥ pāpaḥ sānugaḥ svena pāpmanā' (16); 'api smarati naḥ kṛṣṇo mātaraṃ suhṛdaḥ sakhīn' (17); 'apy āyāsyati govindaḥ sva-janān sakṛd īkṣitum' (18).

statements.claim: Nanda remembered how Krishna had sheltered them from the forest fire, from wind and rain, from the great bull and from the serpent; his heroic deeds and playful sidelong glance; and the rivers, mountains and forests adorned by the touch of Krishna's feet.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.19-21: 'dāvāgner vāta-varṣāc ca vṛṣa-sarpāc ca rakṣitāḥ / smaratāṃ kṛṣṇa-vīryāṇi līlāpāṅga-nirīkṣitam / saric-chaila-vanoddeśān mukunda-pada-bhūṣitān.'

statements.claim: Nanda mused that Krishna and Rama must be the best of the gods come down among men: who else could have broken the great bow tall as three palm trees as an elephant king snaps a staff, or brought down Kamsa — strong as ten thousand elephants — together with the two wrestlers and the royal elephant?
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.22-24: 'manye kṛṣṇaṃ ca rāmaṃ ca prāptāv iha surottamau / kaṃsaṃ nāgāyuta-prāṇaṃ mallau gaja-patiṃ yathā / tāla-trayaṃ mahā-sāraṃ dhanur yaṣṭim ivebha-rāṭ.'

statements.claim: The demons of Krishna's boyhood — Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arishta, Trinavarta, Baka — had fallen to the two brothers one after another.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.25: 'pralambo dhenuko 'riṣṭas tṛṇāvarto bakādayaḥ.'

statements.claim: Yashoda listened and wept as Nanda recounted Krishna's deeds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.27-28 (pack): Yashoda, as her son's deeds were narrated, wept; pack excerpt: 'and Yashoda wept as she listened.'

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Nearly every sentence maps to SB 10.46.7-28 verse-by-verse; only sensory connective color (Uddhava walking the lanes, 'the old man's questions spilling out') is added.

statements.claim: The omens had begun to appear in Dwaraka — a strange bird on a rooftop, a vessel of milk soured before its time — and then signs that made the city speak in low voices; Krishna read them all and grew quiet.
statements.evidence: Index confirms 'fearful omens in Dwaraka' preceding Krishna's departure, and SB 11.6.39 ('tan nirīkṣya...') has Uddhava 'seeing those [omens]'; the specific examples (bird on a rooftop, soured milk) are generic utpāta flavor not in the excerpted verses — acceptable atmosphere.

statements.claim: Uddhava had lately returned from Vrindavan, carrying Krishna's message to the cowherds and bringing back their longing; Nanda's grief, the gopis' tears and the villagers' devotion were fresh with him.
statements.evidence: Supported by the corpus chain (DKS_0502/DKS_0503 and the canonical Uddhava mission of SB 10.46-47); pack index places this episode after the Vrindavan return arc.

statements.claim: Dwaraka had grown rich and proud; its pride worked like a slow fever — long feasts, quarrels over a look, young Yadu clansmen who had forgotten fear; elders whispered the family had grown too great for the earth to hold it.
statements.evidence: Not in the excerpted verses (SB 11.6.39-49), which begin at Uddhava's plea; the decadence of the Yadavas is standard Bhagavata background for their destruction, and 'the omens seemed to say the same thing' ties it to the pack's omens. Atmosphere, not a contested fact.

statements.claim: Uddhava found Krishna alone and fell at his feet, saying: 'Even for half a moment, Keshava, I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet. Wherever you go, carry me also to your abode.'
statements.evidence: SB 11.6.39-42: Uddhava approached the Lord of lords in a secluded place ('vivikta upasaṅgamya jagatām īśvareśvaram'); pack excerpt (vv. 41-42): 'Lord, even for half a moment I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet; carry me also to your abode.'

statements.claim: Uddhava declared Krishna's pastimes the supreme good fortune of human beings, with nothing in the three worlds beside them, and that he had treasured everything Krishna touched — the bed, the seat, the roads, the river pools, his games, his meals, his garlands, scents, clothes and ornaments.
statements.evidence: SB 11.6.43-45: 'tava vikrīḍitaṃ kṛṣṇa nṛnāṃ parama-maṅgalam / śayyāsanāṭana-sthāna-snāna-krīḍāśanādiṣu / tvayopabhukta-srag-gandha-vāso-'laṅkāra-carcitāḥ.'

statements.claim: Even the ascetics who renounce everything and wear only the wind for clothing wander the paths of action remembering and singing Krishna's deeds; they never touched his hand, and they cannot let him go.
statements.evidence: SB 11.6.46-48: 'vāta-vasanā ya ṛṣayaḥ śramaṇā ūrdhra-manthinaḥ / vayaṃ tv iha mahā-yogin bhramantaḥ karma-vartmasu / smarantaḥ kīrtayantas te kṛtāni gaditāni ca.'

statements.claim: Krishna raised Uddhava up and answered: 'What you have said is exactly my own intent. Brahma, Shiva, and the guardians of the worlds long for my return to heaven. The time has come.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (vv. 49-50): Krishna, addressed by his devoted servant, answered: 'What you have said is exactly my own intent; Brahma, Shiva and the world-guardians long for my return to heaven.' ('Raised him up' and 'the time has come' are minor connective gestures consistent with the reply's content.)

statements.claim: Krishna granted Uddhava his prayer — he would not be left behind — and then began to instruct him, as a teacher to a beloved disciple, about the self, the world and the way to freedom.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Krishna, granting his wish, begins to instruct him'; the instruction proper unfolds in the following SB chapters (11.7+), matching the corpus chain to DKS_0505.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. The core dialogue (Uddhava's plea, Krishna's reply) is rendered almost verbatim from SB 11.6.39-49; opening omen-and-city mood is connective atmosphere.

statements.claim: Krishna tells Uddhava the story of King Yadu and the avadhuta: 'Listen... I will tell you what freedom looks like.'
statements.evidence: SB 11.7 is Krishna's instruction to Uddhava; 11.7.23: 'atrāpy udāharantīmam itihāsaṃ purātanam' — here they cite this ancient history — introducing the avadhuta narrative; the pack excerpt quotes the frame.

statements.claim: There was a king named Yadu, of the line of Nahusha, and one day a wandering brahmin — an avadhuta who had put aside everything — came down the road where his party had halted in a forest.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.24: 'avadhūtaṃ dvi-jaṃ kañcic carantam akuto-bhayam' (a certain twice-born avadhuta wandering fearlessly); Yadu is named ('śrī-yadur uvāca') and addressed as 'nāhuṣātmaja' (son of Nahusha); index location: 'a forest road.'

statements.claim: The avadhuta owned nothing and feared nothing, and there was a serenity in him unlike anything Yadu had seen at court.
statements.evidence: Fearlessness is supported ('akuto-bhayam', 'afraid of no one' in Yadu's later speech); the contrast with Yadu's court is interpretive connective color building on verses 26-29.

statements.claim: Yadu spoke of people burning in the fire of desire and greed, and asked the avadhuta: 'Men spend their lives in dharma, wealth, pleasure, and the itch of curiosity... But you are capable, wise, skilled, fortunate; your speech is like nectar; for those who ask, you are the very cause of joy. You act like a child, a madman, a ghost — and yet you are a sage. How did you gain such wisdom?'
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.26-29: 'prāyo dharmārtha-kāmeṣu vivitsāyāṃ ca mānavāḥ / tvaṃ tu kalpaḥ kavir dakṣaḥ su-bhago 'mṛta-bhāṣaṇaḥ / janeṣu dahyamāneṣu kāma-lobha-davāgninā / tvaṃ hi naḥ pṛcchatāṃ brahmann ātmany ānanda-kāraṇam'; pack excerpt: Yadu asked, 'You act like a child, a madman, a ghost, and yet you are a sage; how did you gain such wisdom?'

statements.claim: The avadhuta answered that he has twenty-four gurus, naming them: earth, wind, sky, water, fire, the moon, the sun; the pigeon, the python, the ocean; the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey-gatherer; the deer, the fish, Pingala, the osprey; the child, the maiden, the arrow-maker, the serpent, the spider, the cricket.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.32-35: 'pṛthivī vāyur ākāśam āpo 'gniś candramā raviḥ... ete me guravo rājan catur-viṃśatir āśritāḥ / yato yad anuśikṣāmi'; the pack's rendered excerpt lists the identical twenty-four, in the same order, including Pingala, the osprey (kurara) and the cricket (peśaskṛt).

statements.claim: Yadu's inner reaction — surprise that his teachers include a python, a fish, a maiden, and a woman named Pingala — and his request 'Then teach me.'
statements.evidence: Pingalā is indeed feminine (SB 11.8's famous courtesan), but Yadu's musings and his explicit 'teach me' request are connective narration; the lessons follow directly in the text (11.7.36+) in response to his question.

statements.claim: The avadhuta began with the first of his teachers: the earth itself.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.36ff opens the sequence of lessons with the earth; chain to DKS_0506 ('The earth taught me forbearance').

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. The 24-guru list matches the pack's list exactly and in order; the court-burden color in the opening is generic connective framing.

statements.claim: The earth taught forbearance: every being tramples her — beasts and men, armies, cattle, cart-wheels — morning and evening, yet she never strays from her course; so the wise one, though the world treads on him, does not leave his path.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.36: 'bhūtair ākramyamāṇo 'pi dhīro daiva-vaśānugaiḥ' — though pressed upon by beings, the steadfast one does not deviate; pack index: earth = forbearance.

statements.claim: The wind taught detachment: it moves everywhere — through palaces, market streets and every corner of every house — and clings to nothing it touches; so the yogi moves among the objects of the senses and remains unattached.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.39: 'viṣayeṣv āviśan yogī nānā-dharmeṣu sarvataḥ' — the yogi entering among sense objects everywhere; pack excerpt: 'Moving among the objects of sense, the yogi remains unattached like the wind.'

statements.claim: The sky taught him to remain unaffected: clouds, rain, smoke and birds cross it and leave no mark; so the wise one dwells among all the bodies of the world, moving and unmoving, hidden in each and touched by none, seeing the one self in all things.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.40-42: 'pārthiveṣv iha deheṣu praviṣṭas tad-guṇāśrayaḥ / antarhitaś ca sthira-jaṅgameṣu brahmātma-bhāvena samanvayena' (hidden in moving and unmoving beings through identity of Brahman and self) and 'tejo-'b-anna-mayair bhāvair meghādyair vāyuneritaiḥ' (clouds driven by wind); pack index: sky = unaffectedness.

statements.claim: The water taught purity: clear by nature, sweet to the taste, wherever it flows it becomes a holy place (a tirtha) for men to bathe in; so the sage, pure in himself, makes everything around him sacred and men's dirt falls from them in his presence.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.43: 'svacchaḥ prakṛtitaḥ snigdho mādhuryas tīrtha-bhūr nṛṇām' — naturally clear, soft, sweet, a tirtha for men; pack excerpt: 'pure and sweet like water.'

statements.claim: The fire taught him to be untainted: whatever it is given — wood, refuse, offerings, filth — it burns and takes no stain; it shines by its own heat and is hard to approach; so the sage is not polluted by what he consumes.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.44: 'tejasvī tapasā dīpto durdharṣodara-bhājanaḥ' — radiant, shining by tapas, hard to approach, an undecaying vessel; pack excerpt: 'untainted by what he consumes, like fire.'

statements.claim: The moon taught waxing and waning: it swells to fullness and thins to a sliver, and both are its own nature; the body's states — birth, youth, age, death, up to the cremation ground — belong to the body, not the self, and the wise one watches them as the moon watches its phases.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.45-49: 'kvacic channaḥ kvacit spaṣṭaḥ...' (the moon sometimes hidden, sometimes visible) and 'visargādyāḥ śmaśānāntā bhāvā dehasya nātmanaḥ' (states from creation to the cremation ground belong to the body, not the self); 'guṇair guṇān upādatte yathā-kālaṃ vimuñcati' (takes up and lets go qualities with time); pack index: moon = waxing and waning.

statements.claim: The sun taught the one soul in many bodies: one sun rises on palace and hut, king and beggar, illumining all; the one self appears in every body, and when a body ends nothing of the light is lost.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.50: 'budhyate sve na bhedena vyakti-stha iva tad-gataḥ' — he awakens in himself without distinction, standing in the many like the one sun; pack excerpt: 'one soul appearing in many bodies, like the sun.'

statements.claim: Yadu's interjections — that the first lesson found its mark, that he had filled his court with the learned and none had told him anything so simply — and that the avadhuta then went on to the eighth teacher, the pigeon.
statements.evidence: The lesson content is fully supported; Yadu's inner reactions are invented psychological connective framing, and the transition to the pigeon as the next guru matches the canonical order (SB 11.7.51ff / chain to DKS_0507).

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. All seven element-lessons track SB 11.7.36-50 in pack order (earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon, sun); only Yadu's reflective interludes are connective.

statements.claim: The python taught contentment: he lies where he happens to be and takes whatever comes within reach — fine food or foul, much or little; if nothing comes he lies still for days without effort, pursuit or complaint; so the sage accepts what chance brings and does not run after more.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.1-2: 'grāsaṃ su-mṛṣṭaṃ virasaṃ mahāntaṃ stokam eva vā / ... śayītāhāni bhūrīṇi nirāhāro 'nupakramaḥ' — the python takes food fine or foul, great or small (that chance brings), and lies for many days without food, without enterprise.

statements.claim: The sage bears a body full of vigor and strength yet does not spend it on striving; his hands do what needs doing but his acts leave no trace on him because they are not born of desire.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.3: 'ojaḥ-saho-bala-yutaṃ bibhrad deham akarmakam' — bearing a body full of ojas, strength and power, yet actionless (free from karma-driven acts).

statements.claim: The ocean taught depth: the rivers pour into it and it does not swell; the rivers dry up and it does not sink; it is so deep none can fathom it and so still none can stir it; whatever pours in or is withheld, its fullness is its own.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.4: 'muniḥ prasanna-gambhīro durvigāhyo duratyayaḥ' — the sage serene, deep, unfathomable, hard to cross — the ocean simile of the pack excerpt: 'which neither swells when rivers pour in nor dries when they do not.'

statements.claim: The sage remains the same whether the world pours gifts on him or leaves him empty-handed; whether his desires are fulfilled or he is left destitute, he is fixed on Narayana alone, and his fullness does not rise or fall with fortune.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.5: 'samṛddha-kāmo hīno vā nārāyaṇa-paro muniḥ' — whether his desires are fulfilled or he is deprived, the sage is fixed on Narayana.

statements.claim: Yadu understood the python's stillness and the ocean's depth as one teaching — freedom comes not from having enough but from not needing anything — and the avadhuta, seeing the lesson had landed, spoke next of the moth and the flame.
statements.evidence: Yadu's synthesis is interpretive connective narration consistent with verses 3-5; the moth as the next guru matches the canonical sequence (SB 11.8.6ff) and the chain to DKS_0509 ('The Moth and the Bee').

notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Both lessons render SB 11.8.1-5 closely; only Yadu's reflective closing is connective.
